prize_parts.citation: for the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep B043 as a single prize part to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The first round confirmed that the whole committee reads the scientific chain the same way: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1 in humans, receptor biology, and then degradation-resistant agonists with large randomized evidence in glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The mechanism is independently replicated and the clinical effect is large, so maturity is not in question. The medical significance of the physiology depends on the step that turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-daily and once-weekly drug, so I read the discovery as one achievement that runs from hormone to therapy. That reading supports one citation, not two awards stitched together, and it keeps the credit within three names. Holst and Drucker are common to every configuration on the table. The disagreement is confined to one seat, and I decide it on the strength of the documented, uncontested record, not on how many members hold each view.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my own configuration is that it leaves out Mojsov, whose identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide may be a discovery-level contribution, and that it places an industrial drug-development scientist in a prize for discovery. Leaving Mojsov out may look unfair if the primary record later shows her work was decisive. Habener is outside every credited list, so every trio is open to the charge of incompleteness. Finally, three members have reached a different trio on principled grounds, and a prize that is very strong on impact could be criticised if it were read as honouring commercial scale and not the discovery.

responses.point: A prize to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov rewards the discovery itself, which is what the prize is for, and keeps the citation scientifically precise; leaving out Knudsen leaves the pharmacology unrecognised.
responses.response: I agree that the prize should be anchored in discovery, and I accept that the citation is cleaner if it is about physiology alone. My difficulty is that your configuration depends on a seat whose basis you say yourself cannot be verified from the supplied material. A citation that names the identification of the active peptide invites a priority challenge from the Habener group, who are not credited. The Knudsen seat rests on a record that nobody disputes. Your question in the chair's summary about a two-part framing is fair, but a two-part prize would force a smaller incretin group, so I would instead write one citation that covers the physiology and its development into long-acting agonists, as an arc and not as two separate achievements.

responses.point: Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group cannot be adjudicated from the evidence, and a Drucker-Holst-Knudsen trio is the defensible fallback if the record proves insufficient.
responses.response: Your fallback is my first choice, and I think the condition you set has been met. Round 1 produced no new primary evidence on who first showed the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, and no member claims to have verified it. If the record is not sufficient to support the condition under which your trio is preferred, the committee should proceed on your own stated fallback. I recognise that your first choice rewards the discovery side more tightly, and I would move toward it only if someone presents verified primary-record evidence, for example the timing and content of the Mojsov and Habener reports, showing that Mojsov's contribution was distinct and decisive.

responses.point: A prize citation framed around the discovery of the hormone's active form and its physiology is the most scientifically defensible reading, and Knudsen's work is industrial drug development.
responses.response: I considered this carefully again, since you hold the preference loosely. Where we agree is that discovery has to come first in the citation and that the industrial setting alone is not a reason to exclude anyone. I would not agree that naming the active form is the safest reading of the record. It is the most exposed to the priority dispute you identify yourself. Knudsen led the analogue programme that gave the first durable GLP-1 agonists, and the acylation strategy and the later semaglutide design are the reason the physiology reached patients at scale. I regard those as a scientific advance and not only as commercial execution. Your concern that the prize could be read as honouring the scale of the drugs is a real risk, and the citation should say the physiology comes first.

responses.point: The prize should reward the physiology and the translation, but the committee has to be sure it recognises the discovery and not the commercial scale of the drugs.
responses.response: I share the concern, and I think the answer is in the wording and in the evidence. The citation should describe a mechanism-based development, so that the weight is on the biology and on the design principle of a degradation-resistant, long-acting receptor agonist. The case for Knudsen rests on an identifiable scientific step, not on sales. You changed your trio from Mojsov to Knudsen in the opening, and I read that as a decision to rely on the uncontested record. I stay with that reading and agree with you that this is not settled, and I would revisit the seat if verified priority evidence changes the record.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record on the first demonstration of the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, and the role of the Habener group, would justify Mojsov in place of Knudsen. Nothing in the first round resolves this.
Whether a single citation can be worded so that the physiology and the long-acting agonist development read as one achievement and not two.
Habener's absence from the credited list means that any B043 trio looks incomplete, and that cannot be remedied under the three-person limit.
Long-term safety and durability of chronic incretin therapy are still accumulating, though I do not consider this a bar to recognition.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented involvement with Drucker, Holst, Knudsen or Mojsov, or with any other credited name on the shortlist. My Karolinska Institutet affiliation and my spatial transcriptomics co-authorship are unrelated to these names. I have previously co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg (count not audited), who is on this committee, but none of that work concerns a credited name on the shortlist, and I do not infer any personal connection from shared institutions or topics.
